name: Lisfranc (tarsometatarsal) injury
populations: athletes in football, rugby and soccer (axial load or twist on a plantarflexed foot)
people with high-energy or crush trauma, including polytrauma
male athletes (ligament injuries predominated in the athlete consensus review)
summary: A midfoot ligament or fracture-dislocation injury at the tarsometatarsal joints, often from axial load on a plantarflexed foot. Easily missed without weightbearing imaging; stability decides treatment and arthritis risk.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Stable injuries: non-weightbearing immobilisation for about 6 weeks, then graduated weightbearing. Unstable injuries need fixation or arthrodesis, and the surgeon's protocol governs

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Athletes with stable, nondisplaced ligament injuries managed nonoperatively mostly return within 6–10 weeks; one pooled athlete review reported 2.8 months versus 4.5 months for bony injuries

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Midfoot pain, pain on midfoot squeeze and inability to bear weight after axial load or a twist through a plantarflexed foot; plantar bruising is a classic sign

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Bilateral weightbearing radiographs first; CT or MRI if radiographs are normal and suspicion remains. Non-weightbearing films missed 24% of injuries in one reader study

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Nunley and Vertullo stages I–III (weightbearing radiograph based); recent reviews favour a stable versus unstable framework

keyFacts.label: Long-term risk
keyFacts.value: Post-traumatic osteoarthritis in about 33% after medial tarsometatarsal injuries in one meta-analysis; non-anatomical reduction was the main modifiable factor

overview:
A Lisfranc injury is damage to the tarsometatarsal (TMT) joints of the midfoot. The term was once reserved for fracture-dislocations of these joints, but it now covers a spectrum, from a purely ligamentous sprain centred on the second TMT joint to a high-energy fracture-dislocation [r1,r2]. Modern imaging shows that subtle injuries are recognised far more often than before, so the true incidence is much higher than older figures suggest [r1]. In athletes the usual mechanism is axial compression, or a twist, through a plantarflexed foot [r3].

The injury is easy to miss. In a reader study, 24% of Lisfranc injuries were missed when only non-weightbearing radiographs were used, and nondisplaced injuries were missed more often than displaced ones [r4]. Delay in diagnosis worsens outcome [r11]. Treatment turns on stability: weightbearing radiographs and CT are the key tools, stable injuries usually do well with immobilisation, and displaced or unstable injuries need surgery [r1]. The stakes are long-term. In a meta-analysis of medial TMT injuries, post-traumatic osteoarthritis developed in about 33% of patients, and non-anatomical reduction was a significant risk factor [r5].

epidemiology.text: No reliable population incidence was identified in the sources reviewed. Reviews agree that the injury is under-recognised, because subtle ligamentous injuries are missed on routine radiographs [r1,r4]. In a 1986 series of 72 patients with 76 TMT fracture-dislocations, 81% were polytrauma patients, which reflects a referral population with high-energy injuries rather than athletes [r6]. In sport, an international consensus and systematic review found that ligament injuries predominated in male athletes [r3]. In a small retrospective athlete series, 15 athletes with midfoot sprains were classified using weightbearing radiographs and bone scintigraphy [r7]. In a Japanese series of 33 subtle injuries with weightbearing radiographs and CT, 7 were Nunley stage I, 23 stage II and 3 stage III [r8].

intrinsic: A plantarflexed foot at the moment of loading, when the midfoot is held by ligaments rather than by the bony arch (mechanism described in athlete consensus; the mechanical explanation is clinical reasoning) [r3]
Male sex in athlete cohorts (ligament injuries predominated in male athletes in the consensus review; participation exposure is not controlled) [r3]
A previous midfoot injury or an incompletely treated earlier Lisfranc injury (clinical observation; not tested in the sources reviewed)
Neuropathy or poor bone quality, which make Charcot change or fracture more likely after a midfoot twist (clinical observation)
extrinsic: Sports in which the foot is fixed or loaded in plantarflexion while another player or the body twists over it: football, rugby, soccer, dance and gymnastics [r3]
Axial load through a plantarflexed foot, such as a missed landing, a fall on the heel or another player landing on the heel [r3]
High-energy and crush trauma, including motor vehicle crashes and falls from height; direct crush injuries did poorly in a classic series [r6]
Missed or delayed diagnosis (modifiable: image early with weightbearing views) [r4,r11]

mechanism.summary: The athlete mechanism is axial compression or a twist through a plantarflexed foot, with the heel raised and the body weight carried through the forefoot and midfoot [r3]. A fall onto the heel, a missed landing or a player landing on the back of the leg loads the midfoot, and the metatarsal bases are forced out of line with the tarsus. The Lisfranc ligament, which ties the second metatarsal base to the medial cuneiform, tears or avulses a fleck of bone, and the gap (diastasis) between the medial cuneiform and the second metatarsal opens. Direct crush injuries and high-energy trauma produce more severe fracture-dislocations and have poorer outcomes [r6].
sequence: The foot is plantarflexed with the heel raised, for example in a relevé, a push-off or a landing on the forefoot [r3].
A sudden axial load arrives through the heel and ankle: a missed landing, a fall onto the heel, or another player landing on the back of the leg [r3].
The body weight twists over a foot that is planted, so the forefoot rotates relative to the hindfoot (textbook mechanism; consensus describes axial compression or twisting) [r3].
The dorsal tarsometatarsal ligaments and capsule fail in tension as the metatarsal bases are forced out of line (standard biomechanics; clinical reasoning).

The Lisfranc ligament between the medial cuneiform and the second metatarsal base ruptures, or a fleck of bone avulses at its attachment; avulsion fragments were present at the attachment sites in 93.9% of subtle injuries on CT [r8].
The second metatarsal base is no longer held to the medial cuneiform. Under load the gap widens and the arch can lose height [r7].
The athlete has midfoot pain and swelling, and cannot push off or bear weight; plantar bruising follows [r3].

variants.name: Axial load on a plantarflexed foot (indirect, athletic)
variants.description: The most common sports mechanism: a fall on the heel or a landing on the forefoot with the foot in plantarflexion [r3]. It produces ligamentous or mixed injuries that may be nondisplaced on non-weightbearing films [r4].

variants.name: Twisting (rotational) injury through a fixed foot
variants.description: The forefoot is fixed or planted while the body rotates, so the TMT joints are stressed in abduction and rotation. The athlete consensus lists a twist through a plantarflexed foot as a core mechanism [r3].

variants.name: High-energy or crush injury
variants.description: Direct crush trauma and polytrauma produce displaced fracture-dislocations; in a classic series direct crush injuries did poorly, and the quality of the initial reduction was the major determinant of result [r6].

variants.name: Ligamentous versus bony (avulsion or fracture) injury
variants.description: In athletes, ligament injuries predominate [r3]. A small avulsion fragment from the ligament attachment (the fleck sign) is present in most subtle injuries on CT [r8]. Bony injuries took longer to return to sport (4.5 versus 2.8 months) [r3].

variants.name: Missed injury with late presentation
variants.description: Pain with weightbearing continues for weeks after a presumed sprain. Delay in diagnosis has a negative effect on outcome [r11].

anatomy.text: The Lisfranc, or tarsometatarsal, joint complex links the three cuneiforms and the cuboid to the five metatarsal bases. It is the keystone of the midfoot arch: the second metatarsal base sits recessed between the medial and lateral cuneiforms, and the unique bony and ligamentous anatomy confers strength to the complex [r9]. The Lisfranc ligament runs from the lateral side of the medial cuneiform to the medial side of the second metatarsal base, and no ligament joins the first and second metatarsal bases directly. Dorsal, interosseous and plantar ligaments bind the other bases; the plantar ligaments are stronger than the dorsal ones (standard anatomy, not cited to a single source). The injury is most often described as centred on the second TMT joint [r2]. The first (medial) column is the most mobile and the second and third columns are rigid, so injuries to the medial columns have the strongest effect on arch stability (clinical reasoning).

structures.name: Lisfranc ligament (interosseous, medial cuneiform to second metatarsal base)
structures.role: The main tie between the medial column and the rigid central columns; its failure allows diastasis between the medial cuneiform and the second metatarsal base [r8,r9]

structures.name: Second metatarsal base
structures.role: The recessed keystone of the TMT joint; the site of the 'fleck sign' avulsion [r8]

structures.name: Dorsal tarsometatarsal ligaments and capsule
structures.role: Thinner restraints on the dorsal surface; they fail in tension when the metatarsal bases are forced dorsally (standard anatomy)

structures.name: Plantar tarsometatarsal ligaments
structures.role: Stronger restraint on the plantar surface; plantar injury is associated with loss of arch height on weightbearing views [r7]

structures.name: Medial cuneiform and first metatarsal
structures.role: The medial column; it moves more than the central columns and anchors the Lisfranc ligament at one end [r9]

structures.name: Peroneus longus and tibialis anterior
structures.role: Insert on the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base and support the arch dynamically (standard anatomy; clinical reasoning)

structures.name: Dorsalis pedis artery and deep peroneal nerve
structures.role: Run on the dorsum of the midfoot close to the base of the first and second metatarsals; displaced injuries can threaten them (standard anatomy)

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
The injury is a failure of the ligament complex that holds the metatarsal bases to the tarsus. A mild injury is a sprain of the Lisfranc ligament and the dorsal and plantar capsule with no displacement. A more severe injury is a complete rupture, or a fracture of the bone at the ligament attachment, which allows diastasis and loss of arch height on weightbearing [r7,r8]. Stability, rather than the anatomical pattern, determines treatment: the original anatomy-based classifications were limited as tools for guiding treatment, and current reviews favour a stability-based approach in which weightbearing radiographs and CT identify displacement under load [r1,r11].

The consequences of persistent malalignment fall on the articular surfaces. In the classic series, the quality of the initial reduction was the major determinant of the result, and tarsal instability and late degenerative joint disease caused most of the symptoms [r6]. In a meta-analysis of 686 patients with medial TMT injuries, post-traumatic osteoarthritis occurred in about 33% at a mean follow-up of about 60 months, non-anatomical reduction was the significant single risk factor, and Myerson type C or higher injuries had more severe osteoarthritis [r5].

structures.name: Lisfranc ligament
structures.effect: Sprain, partial tear, complete rupture or avulsion from its bony attachment; the key structure in subtle injuries [r8]

structures.name: Dorsal TMT ligaments and capsule
structures.effect: Tear as the metatarsal bases are displaced; weightbearing CT was particularly sensitive for dorsal ligament damage [r14]

structures.name: Plantar TMT ligaments and capsule
structures.effect: In Nunley stage III injuries the arch height is lost; plantar capsular avulsions were common on CT [r7,r8]

structures.name: Second metatarsal base and medial cuneiform
structures.effect: Avulsion fragments (fleck sign), impaction or fracture at the ligament attachment sites [r8]

structures.name: Articular cartilage of the TMT joints
structures.effect: Impact damage and ongoing malalignment lead to post-traumatic osteoarthritis [r5,r6]

structures.name: Soft tissue and neurovascular structures
structures.effect: Swelling, plantar bruising and, in displaced or high-energy injuries, risk to the dorsalis pedis artery and compartments of the foot (standard anatomy; clinical reasoning)

muscles.name: Peroneus longus and tibialis anterior
muscles.effect: Pain inhibition and disuse weakness reduce dynamic support of the first ray and the arch. Restore this once weightbearing is allowed (clinical reasoning).

muscles.name: Intrinsic foot muscles
muscles.effect: Disuse atrophy in a boot or cast reduces arch support during push-off; short-foot and intrinsic control are rebuilt before running (clinical reasoning).

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius–soleus
muscles.effect: Immobilisation causes calf atrophy, and the forefoot load at push-off then rises on a still-healing midfoot. Calf capacity is rebuilt before running and jumping.

muscles.name: Hip and trunk muscles
muscles.effect: Deconditioning during the unloaded phase affects landing mechanics; maintain strength with non-weightbearing training.

cellular.description: Haematoma and oedema form in the midfoot; platelets, neutrophils and macrophages clear debris and release signals.
Fibroblasts lay down disorganised type III collagen and new capillaries. In stable injuries this is the period of non-weightbearing immobilisation [r1,r11].

Collagen is reorganised along lines of load. A healed ligament is generally weaker than the original (typical ligament healing), and displaced or unstable injuries need surgery to restore alignment [r1,r3].
If the joint heals out of alignment, cartilage degenerates and post-traumatic osteoarthritis develops in about one in three patients after medial TMT injuries [r5].

systems.effect: Loss of the midfoot keystone flattens the arch, alters forefoot loading and can overload the ankle and hindfoot over time (clinical reasoning).
The dorsalis pedis artery crosses the dorsum of the foot, and high-energy or crush injuries risk vascular compromise and compartment syndrome of the foot (standard anatomy; clinical reasoning).

Deep peroneal nerve irritation and the guarding of a painful foot change gait and proprioception for weeks. In one series, patients in the acute phase did not place weight on the injured foot, so weightbearing views can under-read the severity [r8].
Haemarthrosis and soft-tissue oedema produce diffuse midfoot swelling with plantar bruising, which usually peaks within days.
Elite and professional athletes and dancers face a high return demand, which can push loading ahead of ligament healing and lead to a missed or poorly managed injury [r3].

grading.system: Nunley and Vertullo stages I–III (athletes, weightbearing radiographs), within a stability-based framework

grades.description: Midfoot pain, tenderness at the TMT joints and no diastasis on weightbearing radiographs, with the injury shown by a bone scan in the original series; undisplaced [r7].
grades.prognosis: Managed nonoperatively in the original athlete series [r7]; in the consensus, stable nondisplaced injuries with intact ligaments on MRI may be managed nonoperatively with close monitoring [r3]

grades.grade: Stage II: diastasis without loss of arch height
grades.description: Diastasis between the first and second metatarsal bases on weightbearing views, with no loss of arch height on the lateral view [r7].
grades.prognosis: Anatomic reduction and fixation in the original series [r7]; the reported cut-off for diastasis ranged from 1 to 3 mm, most often 2 mm or more, across 58 studies [r10]

grades.grade: Stage III: diastasis with loss of arch height
grades.description: Diastasis with loss of arch height on the weightbearing lateral view, measured as the distance between the plantar aspect of the first cuneiform and the plantar aspect of the fifth metatarsal [r7,r8].
grades.prognosis: Anatomic reduction and fixation in the original series; across all stages the series reported an excellent outcome in 93% of 15 athletes at an average of 27 months [r7]

grades.description: Stable (no displacement on weightbearing views and, where used, intact ligaments on MRI) versus unstable (diastasis, subluxation or displacement). Reviews favour this over the older anatomical classifications, which were limited as guides to treatment [r1,r11].
grades.prognosis: Stable injuries have good outcomes with immobilisation; displaced or comminuted injuries need surgery [r1]

grades.description: An anatomy-based classification of fracture-dislocations (types A to C and higher). In the meta-analysis, Myerson type C or higher injuries had more severe post-traumatic osteoarthritis [r5].
grades.prognosis: Higher type: worse arthritis [r5]. The quality of the initial reduction was the major determinant of result in the original series [r6]

timeframes.summary: Stable injuries are immobilised and not weightbearing for about 6 weeks, then loaded gradually [r1,r11]. Athletes with stable, nondisplaced ligament injuries managed nonoperatively mostly return within 6–10 weeks, whereas bony injuries took longer; surgical injuries follow the surgeon's protocol [r3].

healing.description: Haematoma, oedema and pain. Elevate, protect and obtain weightbearing imaging early (typical ligament healing).
Immobilisation and non-weightbearing for about 6 weeks in stable injuries; fixation and the surgeon's weightbearing plan in unstable injuries [r1,r11].
Graduated weightbearing in a boot then a stiff-soled shoe, with calf and foot strengthening [r11].

healing.phase: Late remodelling and return to loading
healing.description: Collagen matures over months. Impact, jumping and sport are reintroduced by criteria; a ligament is rarely as strong as before (typical ligament healing).

milestones.label: End of non-weightbearing immobilisation (stable injury)
milestones.note: Immobilisation and non-weightbearing for six weeks is the most reliable treatment of stable injuries [r1]

milestones.label: Earliest return in the athlete consensus window
milestones.note: Most athletes with stable, nondisplaced ligament injuries returned within 6–10 weeks [r3]

milestones.label: Upper end of the consensus return window
Mean return to sport, ligament injuries in athletes
milestones.note: 2.8 months in the systematic review within the consensus [r3]

milestones.label: Mean return to sport, bony injuries in athletes

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based, never time-based. In the athlete consensus, most athletes with stable, nondisplaced ligament injuries returned within 6–10 weeks and 96.8% returned to sport, at 2.8 months for ligament injuries versus 4.5 months for bony injuries [r3]. Unstable or displaced injuries need fixation, and the protocol and return depend on the surgeon and the procedure; no validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria were identified [r18].

symptoms: Midfoot pain after a twist or axial load through a plantarflexed foot, often with a feeling that the foot has been 'sprained'
Inability or marked difficulty bearing weight, or pain on pushing off and on rising onto the toes [r3]
Swelling across the dorsum of the midfoot
Pain that persists for weeks beyond a typical sprain, or recurs when weightbearing starts (subtle or missed injury) [r11]
Pain on twisting the forefoot, going up stairs or wearing rigid-soled shoes
signs: Tenderness over the TMT joints, especially the first and second, and across the dorsum of the midfoot [r3]
Swelling of the dorsum and plantar ecchymosis (a classic sign; no accuracy data were identified in the sources reviewed)
Pain on midfoot squeeze and on passive forefoot abduction and pronation with the heel fixed [r3]
Pain and inability to complete a single-leg heel raise, and an antalgic gait with reduced push-off
In severe injuries: visible deformity, a widened forefoot or arch collapse, and neurovascular changes in the foot

subjective: Mechanism: axial load or a twist through a plantarflexed foot, a missed landing, a fall onto the heel, a player landing on the heel, or crush or high-energy trauma [r3,r6]
Ability to bear weight and walk four steps at the time of injury and now; pain may prevent weightbearing at the first visit [r8]
Sport, position, level and season timing; dancers' pointe demands; goals and attitude to surgery
Previous midfoot or foot injuries, earlier 'sprain' that has not settled, prior surgery or arthritis
Other injuries (polytrauma) and signs of neurovascular compromise
Diabetes, neuropathy, smoking and medications that affect bone and ligament healing; occupation and footwear
observation: Dorsal midfoot swelling and bruising, including plantar ecchymosis
Gait: antalgic with reduced push-off; ability to weight-bear
Arch height and forefoot position compared with the other side, standing and seated
Skin integrity, tenting or open wounds, colour and capillary refill of the toes
palpation: Each TMT joint, especially the first and second, and the dorsal midfoot
The medial cuneiform and base of the second metatarsal (the Lisfranc ligament attachments)
The navicular, cuboid and fifth metatarsal base for associated injuries
The dorsalis pedis pulse and the sensation distribution of the deep peroneal nerve
rangeOfMotion: Ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion (usually preserved but painful)
Forefoot abduction and pronation, with the hindfoot fixed: pain at the TMT joints
Great toe and lesser toe motion
strength: Single-leg heel raise: pain and weakness are expected early; do not test if a displaced injury is suspected
Peroneus longus (first ray plantarflexion and eversion) and tibialis anterior
Intrinsic foot strength: short-foot and toe flexion
neuro: Sensation over the dorsum of the foot and first web space (deep peroneal nerve)
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses and capillary refill
Signs of compartment syndrome in a high-energy injury (see red flags)
functional: Gait and weight-bearing tolerance in a boot or shoe
Single-leg heel raise, then hop and landing tests only once the foot is stable and pain-free
Dancers: relevé and demi-pointe tolerance; athletes: running, jumping and cutting (late)

specialTests.name: Midfoot squeeze (compression) test
specialTests.purpose: Provoke pain through the injured TMT joints
specialTests.procedure: Squeeze the medial and lateral borders of the midfoot together, then compare with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of midfoot pain. Pain on squeeze, midfoot tenderness and inability to bear weight were agreed diagnostic findings in the athlete consensus [r3]. No accuracy figures were identified.

specialTests.name: Piano-key test (first and second ray stress)
specialTests.procedure: Hold the hindfoot, grasp the head of the second (or first) metatarsal and move it dorsally and plantarly, then compare with the other side. Omit if a displaced injury or fracture is suspected.
specialTests.positive: Pain, or more movement than the other foot. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Forefoot pronation-abduction stress test
specialTests.purpose: Reproduce pain from a Lisfranc ligament sprain
specialTests.procedure: Fix the heel in one hand and abduct and pronate the forefoot with the other, gently and within tolerance.
specialTests.positive: Pain at the second TMT joint. A positive test is not specific for ligament rupture, and no accuracy figures were identified.

specialTests.name: Single-leg heel raise and weightbearing tolerance
specialTests.purpose: Check functional loading of the plantarflexed midfoot
specialTests.procedure: Ask the patient to stand on the injured foot and rise onto the toes, if safe.
specialTests.positive: Pain at the midfoot or inability to rise. Inability to bear weight is a consensus diagnostic finding [r3]; no accuracy figures were identified.

clinicalRules.name: Ottawa foot rules (screening for radiographs)
clinicalRules.description: Foot radiographs are needed after an acute midfoot injury if there is bone tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal or the navicular, or inability to take four steps. They are designed to identify fractures and they do not exclude a subtle Lisfranc injury, so a patient who cannot weight-bear after a midfoot twist needs weightbearing views (clinical reasoning) [r3].

clinicalRules.name: Weightbearing radiographic alignment checks
clinicalRules.description: Bilateral weightbearing anteroposterior, oblique and lateral films. Check the congruence between each metatarsal base and its tarsal bone, and measure the first to second metatarsal base (M1–M2) or medial cuneiform to second metatarsal base (C1–M2) distance against the other foot [r12,r3]. A diastasis of 2 mm or more was the most common surgical threshold across 58 studies, with cut-offs between 1 and 3 mm [r10].

clinicalRules.name: Stability decision
clinicalRules.description: Classify as stable (no displacement under load, intact ligaments on MRI where used) or unstable (diastasis, subluxation, fracture displacement). Stable injuries are immobilised; unstable injuries are referred for fixation or arthrodesis [r1,r3].

outcomeMeasures.name: AOFAS Midfoot Scale
outcomeMeasures.use: Clinician-rated midfoot outcome; the main outcome in the randomised trial of primary arthrodesis versus fixation [r13]

outcomeMeasures.name: Visual analogue scale (VAS) pain
outcomeMeasures.use: Pain at rest and on loading; used in the trial and meta-analyses [r13,r16]

outcomeMeasures.name: Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM), including the sport subscale
outcomeMeasures.use: Self-reported function and readiness for sport

outcomeMeasures.name: Return to preinjury activity rate and hop and calf-raise symmetry
outcomeMeasures.use: Return to activity was reported in the arthrodesis versus fixation reviews [r16,r17]; symmetry measures are used to guide return in the clinic (clinical convention)

imaging.indication: First-line imaging when a Lisfranc injury is suspected; the athlete consensus agreed on bilateral weightbearing films for initial imaging [r3]
imaging.findings: Diastasis between the first and second metatarsal bases or medial cuneiform and second metatarsal base, loss of congruence, the fleck sign and loss of arch height. In a reader study of 100 sets of non-weightbearing films, mean sensitivity was 76.1% and specificity 85.3%, sensitivity for subtle injuries was 65.4% versus 87.1% for severe injuries, and 24% of injuries were missed [r4]. Weightbearing improves detection of subtle injury [r12]. Pain may prevent weightbearing at the first visit [r8].

imaging.indication: Normal or equivocal radiographs with suspicion, suspected fractures, or planning; low-grade instability [r3]
imaging.findings: CT detects nondisplaced fractures and minimal osseous subluxation better than radiographs [r12]; avulsion fragments at the ligament attachment sites were present in 93.9% of subtle injuries [r8]. Weightbearing CT was more sensitive than conventional CT for subtle Lisfranc instability in a systematic review of 9 studies [r14].

imaging.indication: Low-grade or suspected ligamentous injury with normal weightbearing films; used by the consensus to confirm intact ligaments before nonoperative care [r3]
imaging.findings: Best of the modalities for ligament abnormality, but its utility for detecting subtle instability needs further investigation [r12].

imaging.indication: An adjunct where weightbearing films are not tolerated; accuracy unproven in a systematic review [r12]
imaging.findings: In one small study of 25 patients, cut-offs for the dorsal and articular C1–M2 distances of 9.3 mm and 2.1 mm gave sensitivities of 0.88 and 0.76 and specificities of 0.72 and 0.96 [r15].

differentials.name: Midfoot sprain without instability
differentials.distinguishing: Pain at the midfoot with no diastasis on weightbearing films and intact ligaments on MRI. It is the benign end of the same spectrum, and it can only be confirmed with weightbearing imaging [r3].

differentials.name: Metatarsal stress fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Gradual forefoot pain at a metatarsal shaft or neck, rather than an acute midfoot twist, and no TMT diastasis. Image to confirm.

differentials.name: Navicular stress fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Insidious dorsal midfoot ache at the 'N-spot' with sprinting and jumping; MRI or CT shows the fracture and the TMT joints are normally aligned.

differentials.name: Fifth metatarsal base fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness at the lateral border of the foot at the fifth metatarsal base after an inversion injury; the Lisfranc injury is at the medial TMT joints.

differentials.name: Lateral ankle sprain
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament; midfoot squeeze and TMT stress are negative. The two can coexist.

differentials.name: Cuboid, cuneiform or other midfoot fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness over the individual bone with a fracture line on CT; midfoot fractures can coexist with a Lisfranc injury, so image the whole midfoot (clinical reasoning).

differentials.name: Charcot neuroarthropathy of the midfoot
differentials.distinguishing: A warm, swollen, relatively painless midfoot in a person with diabetes or neuropathy, often after minor trauma; needs urgent specialist care (standard clinical teaching).

redFlags: Open wound, severe deformity, a cold or pale foot or absent pulses, or a tense swollen foot with escalating pain out of proportion to the injury: send to emergency (vascular compromise, compartment syndrome).

Midfoot pain and inability to bear weight after axial load or a twist, with normal non-weightbearing radiographs: do not treat as a sprain. Arrange weightbearing views, CT or MRI, because 24% of injuries are missed on non-weightbearing films and delay worsens outcome [r4,r11].

Displacement, diastasis, fracture-dislocation, loss of arch height or comminution on any imaging: refer urgently to an orthopaedic foot and ankle surgeon, because displaced and unstable injuries need surgery [r1,r3].
High-energy mechanism, crush injury or polytrauma: assume a severe injury, check the neurovascular status and refer; direct crush injuries did poorly in a classic series [r6].

Persistent midfoot pain, swelling, flattening of the arch or a progressive forefoot deformity after 6 weeks of treatment: suspect instability or missed injury and refer for repeat weightbearing imaging [r11].
Diabetes, neuropathy or a warm swollen painless midfoot: suspect Charcot neuroarthropathy and refer for specialist foot care.
After surgery: fever, wound redness or discharge, calf pain or breathlessness, or new numbness over the dorsum of the foot: arrange urgent review.

management.principles: Diagnose early, then classify the injury as stable or unstable, because stability decides the pathway [r1,r11]. Stable injuries (no displacement on weightbearing views and, where used, intact ligaments on MRI) are managed with immobilisation and non-weightbearing for about 6 weeks, then graduated weightbearing [r1,r3,r11]. Displaced or comminuted injuries need surgery; open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) is the most common approach, with a consensus towards bridge plating [r1]. Primary arthrodesis is a niche option for acute injuries: a randomised trial in primarily ligamentous injuries and a pooled analysis of acute injuries favour it, but long-term effects are unknown [r1,r13,r16]. Flexible fixation is promising but rests on low-quality, single-arm evidence [r17]. Restoring and maintaining anatomical alignment is the goal because non-anatomical reduction raises the arthritis risk [r5,r7]. Physiotherapy protects the foot, maintains fitness, and rebuilds the foot and calf in stages.

medical.name: Immobilisation and non-weightbearing (stable injuries)
medical.description: A non-weightbearing cast or boot for about 6 weeks, followed by graduated weightbearing. A review described this as the most reliable treatment for stable injuries [r1], and a simplified algorithm made the same recommendation after stability had been checked on weightbearing films [r11]. In athletes, the consensus agreed that stable, nondisplaced injuries with intact ligaments on MRI may be managed nonoperatively with close monitoring [r3].

medical.name: Open reduction and internal fixation (displaced or unstable injuries)
medical.description: Anatomical reduction with screws, or dorsal bridge plating, which the review described as the consensus; results vary, particularly in high-energy injuries [r1]. Restoring alignment was the key to treatment in the original athlete series, and the quality of the initial reduction determined the result in the classic series [r7,r6]. Rigid fixation was commonly followed by planned hardware removal (86.0% of ORIF patients in one pooled analysis, mostly from single-arm studies) [r17].

medical.name: Primary arthrodesis of the medial two or three rays
medical.description: In a randomised trial of 41 patients with primarily ligamentous injuries, the mean AOFAS Midfoot score at two years was 88 after arthrodesis versus 68.6 after ORIF, and 5 patients in the ORIF group needed later arthrodesis for pain, deformity or osteoarthrosis [r13]. In a meta-analysis of 18 studies, return to preinjury activity was 79.2% versus 65.7%, post-traumatic arthritis 2.8% versus 17.3% and unplanned reoperation 14.7% versus 38.3% in favour of arthrodesis; its long-term effects, including adjacent joint arthritis, are largely unknown in young and active patients [r16]. A review still described it as a niche option for acute injuries [r1], and for bony unstable injuries another review judged that more research was needed before one method could be advocated [r11].

medical.name: Flexible (suture-button) fixation
medical.description: Allows treatment of ligamentous injuries while preserving joint motion. A pooled analysis of mostly single-arm studies reported better scores and fewer complications than ORIF, but the authors rated the evidence low quality [r17]. The review noted promising early findings and a need for comparative studies [r1].

medical.name: Emergency reduction and neurovascular assessment (displaced, high-energy injuries)
medical.description: Urgent assessment and reduction for a dislocated, ischaemic or compartment-threatened foot, followed by definitive surgical planning. Direct crush injuries have poorer outcomes [r6].

medical.name: Analgesia, elevation and ice
medical.description: Short-term pain control and elevation in the first days.

physio.name: Early recognition, imaging referral and education
physio.description: Suspect the injury after a midfoot twist or axial load, obtain bilateral weightbearing imaging, and explain the stability decision and the long-term arthritis risk. This guards against delayed diagnosis, which worsens outcome [r4,r11].

physio.name: Protected loading and cross-training
physio.description: Follow the cast, boot and surgeon's weightbearing plan exactly; maintain hip, trunk, upper-body and cardiovascular fitness with non-weightbearing training (clinical convention; no trial of exercise during immobilisation was identified).

physio.name: Graduated weightbearing and gait retraining
physio.description: After about 6 weeks in stable injuries, load progressively in a boot then a stiff-soled shoe [r11]. A single post-operative case report described the exercise, functional progression and return-to-sport criteria used after Lisfranc fixation in a high school football player [r18].

physio.name: Calf, peroneus longus and intrinsic foot strengthening
physio.description: Progressive loading of the calf, the first ray stabilisers and the short-foot muscles once weightbearing is allowed (clinical convention).

physio.name: Criteria-based return to running, jumping and sport
physio.description: Advance on clinical stability, pain and functional tests. In the athlete consensus, return depended on injury type, with ligament injuries returning earlier than bony injuries [r3]. No validated return criteria were identified [r18].

physio.name: Footwear modification
physio.description: A stiff-soled shoe, rocker sole or carbon plate to reduce midfoot bending during push-off in the late stages (clinical convention; no trial of footwear for this injury was identified).

physio.name: Treating a suspected Lisfranc injury as a simple sprain, or relying on non-weightbearing films alone
physio.description: 24% of injuries were missed on non-weightbearing radiographs, nondisplaced injuries more often than displaced ones, and delay in diagnosis has a negative effect on outcome [r4,r11].

physio.name: Early weightbearing, stress testing and impact before stability is confirmed
physio.description: Loading an unstable midfoot risks diastasis and malalignment, which raise the risk of post-traumatic arthritis [r5,r6]. Do not run, hop, push the foot into forced abduction or return to sport before the foot is confirmed stable.

education: A midfoot 'sprain' that cannot bear weight needs weightbearing X-rays, and sometimes a CT or MRI scan. A normal X-ray taken without weight on the foot does not rule out a Lisfranc injury.
Whether the joint is stable decides the treatment. A stable injury heals in a boot or cast with no weight on the foot for about six weeks; an unstable one usually needs an operation.

Keeping the joint in the right position matters for the long term: arthritis in the midfoot develops in about one in three people after these injuries, and is more likely if the joint heals out of alignment.
Recovery is slow and goes in stages. Stay off the foot until told, build up gradually and do not return to sport or dance until the team agrees the foot is stable and strong.
Keep fit with upper-body, core and non-weightbearing work, and bring any new pain, swelling or flattening of the arch to your physiotherapist or surgeon early.
After surgery, follow the weightbearing plan exactly, and report fever, wound problems or calf pain urgently.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based, and it follows the pathway: stable injury in a boot or cast, or post-operative care under the surgeon's protocol. Always follow the surgeon's weightbearing instructions, which override the timeframes below. The rehabilitation literature is thin: one post-operative case report described the exercises and return criteria used, and no validated criteria exist [r18]. The programme therefore follows clinical convention. For stable injuries, the usual start is about 6 weeks of non-weightbearing immobilisation followed by graduated weightbearing [r1,r11]. Dosages and thresholds are typical clinical ranges, not prescriptions from a single source.

stages.name: Protect & preserve
stages.timeframe: Weeks 0–6 (non-weightbearing; surgeon's protocol applies after fixation)
goals: Protect the TMT joints and any fixation
Maintain proximal strength and cardiovascular fitness
Educate on stability and the loading plan
precautions: Follow the non-weightbearing and boot or cast instructions exactly [r1,r11]
No forced forefoot abduction, twisting or toe-off loading
After surgery, monitor the wound, calf and dorsal foot sensation

exercises.name: Quadriceps sets
exercises.cues: Push the back of the knee down

exercises.name: Straight-leg raise
exercises.cues: Lock the knee and lift to the height of the other knee

exercises.name: Side-lying hip abduction (clamshell)
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis still and the foot relaxed

exercises.name: Double-leg glute bridge
exercises.cues: Weight through the heels; keep the injured foot comfortable and protected

exercises.name: Upper-body ergometer or seated circuit
exercises.cues: Keep the injured foot elevated and unloaded

progressionCriteria: Swelling controlled and resting pain at or below 3/10
Weightbearing imaging confirms a stable alignment (or surgeon permits loading)
Surgeon or physician allows graduated weightbearing

stages.name: Graduated loading
goals: Progress weightbearing in a boot, then a stiff-soled shoe
Restore ankle range and early calf control
precautions: Progress by tolerance and the surgeon's schedule; keep foot pain at or below 3/10 and settled the next day (clinical convention)
Avoid toe-off loading, forced forefoot twisting, hopping and running
Stop and report if swelling, arch flattening or midfoot pain increases

exercises.name: Graded weight-shift in a boot
exercises.dosage: 5 × 1 min, several times daily, increasing load as allowed
exercises.cues: Roll through the foot, heel to toe, and keep the arch relaxed and quiet

exercises.name: Ankle range of motion
exercises.cues: Slow and pain-free; no forced forefoot twisting

exercises.name: Seated calf raise
exercises.cues: Press through the ball of the foot; stay within pain limits

exercises.name: Short-foot (arch) activation, seated
exercises.cues: Shorten the foot without curling the toes

exercises.name: Single-leg balance in a boot or stiff shoe
exercises.cues: Soft knee and quiet trunk

progressionCriteria: Full weightbearing in a shoe without a limp
Pain at or below 2/10 with walking and no next-day swelling
Surgeon or clinician confirms stable alignment on weightbearing imaging

stages.name: Strength & foot control
goals: Restore calf, peroneal and intrinsic foot strength
precautions: Confirm stability before impact and toe-off loading
Stop if midfoot pain, swelling or arch collapse returns

exercises.name: Double-leg calf raise, then single-leg
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–12 slow, building to single-leg 3 × 8–12 every second day
exercises.cues: Even weight over the first and fifth toes, full range and a pause at the top

exercises.name: Single-leg calf raise
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–12, 3 s up and 3 s down, every second day
exercises.cues: Keep the arch lifted and do not roll outwards

exercises.name: Step-up and controlled step-down
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level and the knee over the second toe

exercises.name: Resisted peroneus longus and first-ray strengthening with a band
exercises.cues: Press the first toe down and out; slow return

exercises.name: Single-leg balance with perturbation
exercises.cues: Keep the arch active and the weight even across the forefoot

progressionCriteria: Single-leg calf raise × 15 with pain at or below 2/10 and equal height to the other side
Walks 30 min on a firm surface with no midfoot pain or swelling
Stability confirmed clinically and, where needed, on weightbearing imaging
Single-leg stance 30 s without arch collapse or pain

stages.name: Return to run, jump & sport
stages.timeframe: Weeks 12–24+ (criteria-based; athletes with stable ligament injuries often earlier [r3])
goals: Return to running, hopping, jumping and cutting
Dancers: relevé, demi-pointe and pointe loading
Return to team training and competition
Plan a long-term load and footwear strategy
precautions: Add volume and intensity in steps and avoid rushing
Do not return to competition while midfoot pain or swelling persists
Bony injuries and fixation need more time (4.5 versus 2.8 months in athletes) [r3]

exercises.name: Walk–run program
exercises.dosage: 1 min run / 2 min walk for 20 min, 3 times a week, adding running every 1–2 sessions (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Quiet landings and an even load across the whole foot

exercises.name: Single-leg hop in place, forward and lateral
exercises.cues: Soft landing and stick for 2 s

exercises.name: Jump landing and rebound drills
exercises.cues: Land on the whole foot with hips and knees bent

exercises.name: Planned then reactive change of direction
exercises.dosage: 2 sessions a week, increasing speed and angle
exercises.cues: Plant the foot flat, then rotate; avoid twisting on a planted forefoot

exercises.name: Dancers: graded relevé progression
exercises.dosage: Double-leg relevé 3 × 10, then single-leg and demi-pointe, building over 4–8 weeks (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Even weight through the first and second toes; no sickling

exercises.name: Graded team training
exercises.dosage: Partial then full training over 2–3 weeks
exercises.cues: Share the plan with the coach and monitor pain and swelling

progressionCriteria: Full training for at least 2 weeks with pain at or below 1/10 and no next-day swelling
Single-leg hop distance and calf-raise capacity at or above 90% of the other side (clinical convention)
Surgeon or physician confirms stability and union where applicable
Athlete, coach and clinician agree on the return

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria were identified for Lisfranc injuries; the criteria below reflect clinical convention and the athlete consensus [r3,r18]
Stability confirmed: no diastasis or malalignment against the other foot on weightbearing imaging, and surgeon sign-off after any fixation [r1,r3]
Pain-free full weightbearing, walking, running, jumping and cutting at or below 1/10, with no swelling or next-day flare
Calf, hop and balance performance at or above about 90% of the other side (clinical convention)
Dancers: pain-free relevé, demi-pointe and pointe work in the appropriate footwear before returning to full class
Full, unrestricted training for at least 2 weeks, with graded exposure, a footwear plan and a maintenance strength programme in place
tests: Palpation of the TMT joints and pain on midfoot squeeze
Weightbearing radiographs (or weightbearing CT) compared with the other foot, as directed by the surgeon
Single-leg heel raise repetitions, height and pain
Single-leg hop tests (single, triple, side) with pain rating
Weekly training volume and next-day pain and swelling log

prognosis: Outcomes depend on the injury and on the quality of reduction. In the classic series of 52 patients with 55 TMT fracture-dislocations followed for a mean of 4.2 years, 49% had an excellent or good result and 51% a fair or poor result; direct crush injuries did poorly, and the quality of the initial reduction was the major determinant [r6]. In 15 athletes with midfoot sprains treated according to the Nunley and Vertullo stages, 93% had an excellent outcome at an average of 27 months [r7]. Post-traumatic osteoarthritis occurred in about 33% after medial TMT injuries, and non-anatomical reduction raised the risk [r5]. In a randomised trial of ligamentous injuries, the AOFAS Midfoot score at two years was 88 after primary arthrodesis and 68.6 after ORIF, and 5 of 20 ORIF patients needed later arthrodesis [r13]. A meta-analysis found fewer unplanned reoperations (14.7% versus 38.3%) and less post-traumatic arthritis (2.8% versus 17.3%) after primary arthrodesis, with unknown long-term effects [r16]. In athletes, 96.8% returned to sport in the systematic review within the athlete consensus [r3]. Evidence is mostly retrospective, and long-term outcomes of nonoperative care for subtle injuries are less well defined.
prevention: No prevention trials were identified. Early recognition and weightbearing imaging after a midfoot twist or axial load can limit the damage from a missed injury [r4,r11].
Dancers and athletes: practise controlled landings from jumps, with the heel lowering and the whole foot absorbing load (clinical observation; no trial identified).
Review footwear, studs and surfaces for foot-fixation risks in football and rugby (clinical observation).
After a Lisfranc injury, stay out of sport until stability is confirmed, because malalignment and re-injury risk post-traumatic arthritis [r5,r6].
Screen for neuropathy and bone health in people with midfoot injuries after minor trauma (clinical observation).
clinicalPearls: A normal non-weightbearing X-ray does not exclude a Lisfranc injury. In a reader study, 24% were missed and subtle injuries were missed more often (sensitivity 65.4% versus 87.1% for severe injuries) [r4].

Midfoot pain, plantar bruising and inability to bear weight after axial load or a twist through a plantarflexed foot is a Lisfranc injury until proven otherwise (clinical teaching). Order bilateral weightbearing views and compare with the other foot [r3,r12].
Look for the fleck sign: a small avulsion fragment at the second metatarsal base or medial cuneiform. Avulsion fragments were present in 93.9% of subtle injuries on CT [r8].
The stability decision, not the anatomical pattern, drives treatment: stable injuries are immobilised; displaced or unstable injuries are fixed or fused [r1,r11].
Explain the arthritis risk early. Post-traumatic osteoarthritis occurred in about 33% after medial TMT injuries, and non-anatomical reduction was the main modifiable factor [r5].

Surgical choice is contested: primary arthrodesis did better than ORIF in one RCT of primarily ligamentous injuries and in a pooled analysis, but long-term data are lacking and bony injuries are less clear, so involve the surgeon and the athlete early [r11,r13,r16].

forces.label: Body weight loads the plantarflexed midfoot

captions.text: A dancer jumps and begins to land.
She lands on a fully plantarflexed foot, with the heel raised.
Her whole body weight drives down through the plantarflexed midfoot.
The midfoot is held only by its ligaments, and they take the full load.
She feels a sharp midfoot pain and cannot put weight on the foot.
Zooming into the right foot, viewed from above (dorsal view).

actions.text: Ruptured: M2 is no longer tied to the cuneiform
Bony variant: a fleck of bone avulses

captions.text: The Lisfranc ligament ties the second metatarsal base to the medial cuneiform.
An axial load and twist through the plantarflexed foot stress the tarsometatarsal joints.
The ligament and the dorsal capsule stretch beyond their limit.
The Lisfranc ligament ruptures, and the second metatarsal base shifts away from the cuneiform.
The gap (diastasis) is what weightbearing X-rays and CT look for.
A displaced, unstable foot needs fixation to restore alignment.
In many subtle injuries the ligament pulls a small fleck of bone from its attachment.
A normal X-ray without weight on the foot can miss both patterns.
Healthy ligament: tightly packed, aligned type I collagen fibres.
Loaded: the fibres straighten as the midfoot takes load.
Overload: the axial load and twist push the fibres past their limit.
Failure: fibres rupture, and the second metatarsal base is no longer held.
Haemorrhage: blood fills the gap and the midfoot swells and bruises.
Inflammation: platelets and macrophages clear debris and release repair signals.
Proliferation: fibroblasts lay down disorganised collagen in a protected, non-weightbearing foot.
Remodelling: collagen aligns along the load over months, but unstable injuries need fixation to hold alignment.
